name: Hyperkalaemia

matching.reasoningTemplate: Weakness and bradyarrhythmia with renal impairment suggest hyperkalaemia — an ECG-confirmed emergency.

redFlags: Risk of fatal arrhythmia — treat empirically on ECG changes

clinicalPearls: Hyperkalaemia (plasma K+ ≥5.5 mM) occurs in up to 10% of hospitalised patients; severe hyperkalaemia (>6.0 mM) in ~1% and carries significantly increased mortality (p.401).
Reduced renal K+ excretion is the single most common underlying cause; transcellular shift and reduced tissue uptake act mainly as acute contributors (p.401).

Excess dietary intake alone is a rare cause because the kidney can normally upregulate secretion — but small intake increments can provoke severe hyperkalaemia in susceptible patients (e.g. diabetics with hyporeninaemic hypoaldosteronism and CKD); occult sources include K+-containing salt substitutes (p.401-402).
The ECG changes of hyperkalaemia are notoriously INSENSITIVE, particularly in CKD/ESRD patients — a normal ECG does NOT exclude dangerous hyperkalaemia (p.403).

Hyperkalaemia per se impairs renal acid excretion (K+ competes with NH4+ for TALH reabsorption), so it can itself contribute to metabolic acidosis; restoring normokalaemia often corrects this hyperkalaemic acidosis (p.403).

Hyperkalaemia can produce a type I Brugada ECG pattern (pseudo-RBBB with coved ST elevation in precordial leads); the hyperkalaemic Brugada sign is distinguished from genetic Brugada syndrome by absent P waves, marked QRS widening and an abnormal QRS axis (p.403).
A urine Na+ concentration <20 mM signals that low distal Na+ delivery is limiting K+ excretion, suggesting volume repletion or a loop diuretic may help lower K+ (p.403).
harrison.pathophysiology: Plasma K+ rises when efflux of intracellular K+ outpaces clearance or when renal excretion falls. Acidaemia drives K+ out of cells via effective K+-H+ exchange to buffer extracellular pH — but this shift is seen mainly with non-anion-gap (mineral) and respiratory acidoses; it does NOT occur with the organic anion-gap acidoses (lactic acidosis, ketoacidosis). Hyperosmolality (mannitol, hypertonic saline, IVIG, hypertonic glucose without insulin in diabetics) shifts K+ out by solvent drag. Cationic amino acids (lysine, arginine, epsilon-aminocaproic acid) and Na+/K+-ATPase inhibitors (digoxin and related cardiac glycosides from yellow oleander, foxglove, cane-toad bufadienolide; fluoride) cause efflux. Succinylcholine depolarises muscle via upregulated acetylcholine receptors (contraindicated after burns, neuromuscular injury, disuse atrophy, prolonged immobilisation). Impaired excretion arises from blockade of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone axis, reduced distal Na+/flow delivery, hyporeninaemic hypoaldosteronism, mineralocorticoid resistance, and reduced functioning nephron mass. Cardiotoxicity reflects altered cardiac membrane excitability: mild rises alter repolarisation (T-wave changes), higher levels depress intracardiac conduction (PR/QRS prolongation, P-wave loss, QRS widening, sine wave). (p.401-403)
additionalDifferentials: Hyporeninaemic hypoaldosteronism — common in diabetics, the elderly and renal insufficiency; classically suppressed renin and aldosterone, ~50% with associated acidosis (reduced urinary NH4+, positive urinary anion gap, urine pH <5.5) (p.402)
Primary adrenal insufficiency / Addison's disease (autoimmune or polyglandular endocrinopathy) (p.401-402)
Adrenal infiltration (amyloidosis, metastatic cancer) or adrenal haemorrhage/infarction (e.g. antiphospholipid syndrome) (p.402)
Pseudohypoaldosteronism type I (ENaC or mineralocorticoid receptor defects) and type II / hereditary hypertension with hyperkalaemia (WNK1/WNK4, KLHL3, CUL3 mutations) (p.402)
Hereditary hyperkalaemic periodic paralysis (SCN4A mutations) — weakness with K+ intake or rest after exercise (p.403)
Tubulointerstitial disease affecting the distal nephron (amyloidosis, sickle cell, interstitial nephritis, obstructive uropathy) causing hyperkalaemia out of proportion to GFR (p.402)
Tumour lysis syndrome and rhabdomyolysis — release of intracellular K+ from tissue necrosis (p.402)
infectionMimics: Adrenal insufficiency from infectious causes (HIV — important cause, usually subclinical and may be unmasked by stress, ketoconazole or steroid withdrawal; cytomegalovirus; tuberculosis; disseminated fungal infection) presenting with hyperkalaemia and hyponatraemia (p.402)
nonInfectiousMimics: Pseudohyperkalaemia (factitious hyperkalaemia) — artefactual K+ release during/after venepuncture from fist clenching, marked thrombocytosis/leukocytosis/erythrocytosis with in vitro efflux, cold storage of the sample, or hereditary red-cell membrane transport defects (e.g. SLC4A1/AE1 mutations) (p.401-402)
Acute anxiety at venepuncture with respiratory alkalosis causing redistributive (true but transient) hyperkalaemia (p.402)
additionalInvestigations: Serum electrolytes, BUN, creatinine, serum osmolality, Mg2+ and Ca2+, complete blood count (p.403)
Urinary pH, osmolality, creatinine and electrolytes (urine Na+ <20 mM indicates distal Na+ delivery limits K+ excretion) (p.403)
Transtubular K+ gradient (TTKG) as a bedside index of urinary K+ excretion — expected >7-8 in hyperkalaemia; values <8 suggest tubular resistance/low aldosterone (interpret cautiously) (p.403)
Plasma renin activity and aldosterone, with 9-alpha-fludrocortisone response, to characterise hypoaldosteronism (p.403)
redFlags: Hyperkalaemia is a medical emergency because of its cardiac effects — arrhythmias include sinus bradycardia, sinus arrest, slow idioventricular rhythms, VT, VF and asystole (p.402-403).

ECG progression as a severity cue: tall peaked T waves (5.5-6.5 mM) -> loss of P waves (6.5-7.5 mM) -> widened QRS (7.0-8.0 mM) -> sine-wave pattern (>8.0 mM), heralding impending VF/asystole (p.403).
ECG manifestations mandate urgent treatment; but K+ ≥6.5 mM WITHOUT ECG changes should still be managed aggressively, because ECG findings are an unreliable predictor of cardiac toxicity (p.403-404).

Management principle (knowledge): a three-stage sequence — (1) immediately antagonise cardiac effects (IV calcium stabilises the myocardium by raising the action-potential threshold), (2) shift K+ into cells, (3) remove K+ from the body (p.403-404).
Secondary hyperkalaemic paralysis — ascending paralysis that can include diaphragmatic paralysis and respiratory failure (p.403).
harrison.prognosis: Severe hyperkalaemia (>6.0 mM) is associated with a significantly increased risk of mortality. Cardiac toxicity can progress rapidly to fatal arrhythmia, but is reversible with prompt treatment; hyperkalaemic metabolic acidosis frequently corrects once normokalaemia is restored. (p.401, p.403)
pitfalls: Treating a falsely high K+: failing to exclude pseudohyperkalaemia before intervening (haemolysed sample, fist clenching, extreme thrombo/leuko/erythrocytosis, cold storage) (p.401-402).
Relying on a normal/near-normal ECG to exclude dangerous hyperkalaemia — ECG changes are notoriously insensitive, especially in CKD/ESRD (p.403).

Forgetting drug and dietary causes: ACEi/ARB/renin inhibitors and mineralocorticoid-receptor blockers (spironolactone, eplerenone, drospirenone) — additive in combination; K+-sparing diuretics and the structurally similar antibiotics trimethoprim and pentamidine block ENaC; NSAIDs/COX-2 inhibitors, calcineurin inhibitors and beta-blockers cause hyporeninaemic hypoaldosteronism; heparin/LMWH inhibit aldosterone synthesis (p.402).
Drugs blocking the RAA axis also blunt the adrenal aldosterone response to a rising K+, compounding the effect (p.402).

Anion-gap acidoses (lactic acidosis, ketoacidosis) do NOT shift K+ out by the acidosis mechanism, unlike non-anion-gap and respiratory acidoses — so attributing hyperkalaemia to acidosis in these settings can mislead (p.402).
harrison.severityClassification: By plasma K+: hyperkalaemia ≥5.5 mM; severe >6.0 mM (markedly increased mortality). ECG-correlated severity bands: peaked T waves 5.5-6.5 mM; loss of P waves 6.5-7.5 mM; widened QRS 7.0-8.0 mM; sine-wave pattern >8.0 mM. Emergency treatment is triggered by any ECG change or K+ ≥6.5 mM. (p.401, p.403-404)

cells.text: Diarrhea; external pancreatic or small-bowel drainage; ureterosigmoidostomy, jejunal loop, ileal loop; drugs: calcium chloride (acidifying agent), magnesium sulfate (diarrhea), cholestyramine (bile acid diarrhea)
Proximal RTA (type 2), drug-induced: acetazolamide, topiramate; distal (classic) RTA (type 1), drug-induced: amphotericin B, ifosfamide

Generalized distal nephron dysfunction (type 4 RTA): mineralocorticoid deficiency; mineralocorticoid resistance (autosomal dominant PHA I); voltage defect (autosomal dominant PHA I and PHA II); tubulointerstitial disease
Potassium-sparing diuretics (amiloride, triamterene, spironolactone); trimethoprim; pentamidine; ACE inhibitors and ARBs; nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs; cyclosporine and tacrolimus
Acid loads (ammonium chloride, hyperalimentation); loss of potential bicarbonate (ketosis with ketone excretion); expansion acidosis (rapid saline administration); hippurate; cation exchange resins
